newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal rhinos begin journey to London amid protest.
newsitem.headline: Nepal rhinos begin journey to London amid protest.

text.p: A plane carrying two young one-horned Asian rhinoceroses left Nepal for London on Monday amid protests by environmental activists, officials said.

More than a dozen local environmentalists carrying banners protested outside Kathmandu's Tribhuvan International Airport, demanding greater openness in the government's policy of giving endangered species to foreign countries.

Two cages holding the rhinoceroses were forklifted on to a Lufthansa aircraft, which left on a scheduled flight to London. The animals are due to arrive in Britain on Tuesday after an overnight stop in Frankfurt.

The two female calves, aged 14 to 16 months, are gifts from the Nepali government to the Zoological Society of London, which runs London Zoo and Whipsnade Wild Animal Park in Bedfordshire near London.
In the past Nepal has given 25 rhinoceroses to different countries, including the United States, Germany and Bangladesh.
British officials said the animals would stay at London Zoo until the end of summer, when they would be transferred to Whipsnade where a special centre is being created for them.
Whipsnade curator Nick Lindsay, in Nepal to oversee the rhinos' move, said they would join seven already at the park in an international captive breeding programme.
"This is part of an overall conservation programme where all zoos having the species cooperate to increase the population," Lindsay told Reuters last week.
The rhinoceroses were captured in March by Nepali wildlife experts on elephant-back at the Royal Chitaun National Park, about 100 km (60 miles) south of Kathmandu.
They were kept in quarantine for weeks to ensure they did not catch any diseases before the move to Britain, particularly foot-and-mouth disease, Nepali officials said.
On Sunday, the rhinoceroses were moved by truck from the jungles to the Nepali capital.
The one-horned Asian rhinoceros is found only in the swampy grasslands of India and Nepal.
A total of 466 rhinoceroses were counted in 1994 at the Royal Chitaun National Park, and Nepali experts said the population may have now reached 500.
